segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of what many consider the greatest English novel of the nineteenth century.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fog, its law courts, its orphans and aristocrats and spontaneously combusting rag-and-bone men.
We begin today where Dickens himself begins — with fog.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights, fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners — and, crucially, fog most dense of all in the Court of Chancery.
To help us unpack what that fog conceals and what it reveals, I have three remarkable companions with me today.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don, a lifelong student of Dickens, and — I should say — a man constitutionally resistant to anything he regards as a politicised reading of literature.
For Sir Edmund, Bleak House is above all a novel about moral character, and I suspect he'll have things to say about Esther Summerson that will challenge and delight us in equal measure.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career studying the Victorian institutions that Dickens was so mercilessly anatomising.
He knows what the Court of Chancery actually was — what it smelled like, how it worked, and why it ruined people — and that knowledge will keep us honest.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since, each time finding something new.

She is our close reader — the one most likely to stop mid-sentence, ask us to listen to how a line sounds, and insist that a particular passage is simply one of the finest things written in the English language.

It is a pleasure to be here, and I think there is no more fitting place to begin than with that extraordinary opening — which is, to my mind, one of the most audacious acts of literary scene-setting in the English canon.
Dickens opens not with a character, not with a situation, but with a condition of the atmosphere — and that condition is moral as much as it is meteorological.
He writes — and I think one must hear it aloud to feel its full weight —
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That word — defiled — is doing extraordinary work.

Dickens is not merely describing weather. He is describing a moral contamination that has settled over English society — and he wants us to feel it in our lungs before we understand it with our minds.
Sir Edmund is right that the fog is doing enormous literary work — but I'd add that it is also doing something very precise and historically specific.
Dickens locates the thickest fog not in the rookeries of St Giles or on the Thames — but in Lincoln's Inn Hall, at the very seat of the Court of Chancery.
That is a deliberate and, I'd argue, radical act of targeting.

The Court of Chancery in the 1850s was not an abstraction. It was a real institution that had accumulated centuries of unresolved cases — Jarndyce and Jarndyce is only a slight exaggeration of suits that had run for generations.
Dickens writes that it is a court which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire.
"Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here."
Four words of advice that cost real people, in the real world, everything they had to learn.
What strikes me — every time, even on the fifth reading — is the sheer rhythm of that opening page.
Dickens builds it like an incantation. Fog here, fog there, fog in this place, fog among those people.
By the time he reaches the Lord High Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall, you already feel enclosed by it.
There's a line I find quietly devastating —
"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery."
Groping and floundering. Those are not dignified words for a court of law. That's the point — and Dickens knew exactly what he was doing.
There's a kind of savage glee in his precision there, and I think that's what makes the opening so unforgettable — it's funny and it's furious at the same time.
Caroline is right about the rhythm — but I would gently resist the word 'savage.' Dickens' control here is actually extraordinary.
He does not descend into mere polemic. The fog is, yes, a vehicle for social critique — James has made that admirably clear — but it is also, and I think primarily, a work of imagination.
What Dickens is creating is an atmosphere that a reader inhabits — not an argument that a reader follows.
That is the distinction I would draw between a great novelist and a great pamphleteer. Dickens, at his finest, is always the former.
I'd accept the distinction in principle — while noting that the pamphleteer and the novelist are not always as separable as Sir Edmund suggests.
Dickens serialised Bleak House from 1852 to 1853. The Chancery Reform Act passed in 1852. These things were not coincidences.
He was writing into an ongoing public argument — and the fog was his most powerful rhetorical weapon.
And perhaps that tension — between the imaginative and the polemical — is one we'll be returning to throughout this series.
Because Bleak House is a novel that seems to insist on being read in multiple ways at once — and resists any single key.
In our next segment, we'll move deeper into the fog — into Lincoln's Inn Hall itself, and into the strange double narrative that Dickens chose to tell this story through.
Two voices, two tenses, two kinds of knowledge — and the question of why Dickens needed both.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been spending this episode deep inside Dickens' great, fog-bound masterpiece — its institutions, its minor characters, its extraordinary narrative architecture.
Now we turn to one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads: the ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard is young, charming, genuinely likeable — and Jarndyce versus Jarndyce destroys him by degrees.
It's not a sudden catastrophe. It's an erosion. A slow replacement of everything hopeful with something hollow.
Edmund, you've written and thought a great deal about the moral dimension of this story. Where does Richard's tragedy begin, in your view?
It begins, I think, precisely where Dickens intends us to look — not in Chancery, but in Richard's own character.
This is the distinction I would press upon anyone who reads the novel as purely a social critique.
Richard has a constitutional instability — what an earlier age would have called a want of fixity of purpose — that pre-exists his entanglement with the suit.
Think of those early chapters — his enthusiasm for medicine, then law, then the army. Each profession seized upon and then abandoned.
Jarndyce himself sees it with painful clarity from the very beginning.
He says of Richard, in words that have always struck me as among the most sorrowful in the novel:
"The system — the monstrous system — has its grip on him, and it will not let him go."
Jarndyce understands that the suit does not create the weakness — it finds it, and feeds upon it.
That, to my mind, is Dickens at his most morally precise.
I wouldn't dispute the character analysis — but I'd push back on the sequencing.
Yes, Richard has a susceptible temperament. But what he encounters in Chancery is not a neutral test of that temperament.
Chancery in the eighteen-forties was a system specifically designed — if one can call it design — to protract, to defer, to extract fees at every stage.
The real case of Jennens versus Jennens, which almost certainly informed Dickens, ran for over a century.
Richard is handed a document — the promise of a fortune just beyond his reach — and told it may resolve itself next term, or the term after that.
That is not a test of character. That is an institutionally manufactured form of madness.
Dickens puts it in terms that are almost clinical when Richard's obsession hardens:
"It can't last much longer. The thing must be over soon. We shall come on for a final hearing and get judgment in our favour."
That repetition — the thing must be over, it must be over — is the grammar of a man whose reason is being slowly colonised by false hope.
Chancery didn't merely find a weakness. It manufactured the conditions in which weakness becomes the only rational response.
That is a formidable argument, and I don't dismiss it.
And yet — Ada loves Richard. John Jarndyce loves Richard. Esther watches him with a grief that is almost maternal.
He is surrounded by people who see the danger and who offer him, repeatedly, a way out.
The tragedy is that he cannot take it. Not because the institution prevents him — but because something in him won't permit it.
He becomes, in the end, suspicious even of Jarndyce — imagining that his guardian has an interest in prolonging the suit.
That moment of paranoia is, for me, the true hinge of the tragedy — not the legal machinery, but the moral collapse.
What strikes me — reading it — is how Dickens makes us feel Richard's charm even as we watch him disappear.
He's so vivid in those early chapters at Bleak House. There's a lightness to him, a readiness for life.
And then Esther notices — it's always Esther who notices — that something has changed behind his eyes.
She sees him later in London, and there's that terrible line where she observes that the suit has become his vocation — his entire world.
"He had a clutch upon his interest and hopes. It was not a thing to leave him."
That word — clutch — is so physical. It's a hand around the throat. It's not metaphorical, it's anatomical.
Dickens knows that obsession is not an idea — it is a bodily condition.
And the worst of it is Ada. Ada keeps loving him. Ada marries him secretly. Ada watches him die.
She's one of those characters Dickens doesn't quite know what to do with — and yet that very passivity makes her tragedy real.
The Ada point is important, and it connects to something Esther records — almost without editorialising — about the material circumstances of their marriage.
Richard is drawing on whatever small funds he has, and running into debt, in pursuit of a fortune that the suit dangles before him.
He is not simply deluded — he is financially entrapped. Each step deeper into the suit makes it harder to exit, because now he has real money in it.
It's the logic of a gambler who cannot stop because stopping means acknowledging that the losses are real.
Vholes, the solicitor, is the novel's great portrait of institutional parasitism — a man who feeds calmly and legalistically on Richard's diminishing estate.
Dickens describes him as a man who gives the appearance of eating Richard alive.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself. There is no other principle distinctly, certainly, and consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings."
That's Dickens speaking through the narrator — not subtly — but it is precisely accurate as legal history.
Vholes isn't evil in a theatrical sense. He's compliant. And that compliance is what makes him monstrous.
Vholes has that extraordinary moment where he lays his gloves on Richard's papers — as if he's laying a claim.
It's such a precise piece of physical writing. Dickens always gives the sinister characters a gesture, a tic, something with the hands.
But I keep coming back to the scene near the end — when Esther visits Richard in his rooms and finds him gaunt, obsessive, still certain the next hearing will resolve everything.
He says to Esther something that breaks my heart every time.
"I have been grievously mistaken. I have done what I meant not to do. I have been led step by step."
He knows. That's the terrible thing. By the end he knows what has happened to him.
The self-awareness comes too late to save him — but it doesn't come too late for us to feel the full weight of it.
That passage cuts through every argument about causation — institutional or moral — and lands somewhere more painful than either.
What Richard finally acknowledges is not simply that he has been wronged — but that he has participated in his own destruction.
That is the note that separates Dickens from his own polemics. He cannot quite let the system bear all the guilt.
And so Richard's death scene has this quality — almost Shakespearean — of clarification under mortal pressure.
He tells Esther in his last hours — and I find this one of the most luminous moments in the novel:
"I have done a world of harm. But I have loved Ada truly."
The simplicity of that — after five hundred pages of complication — is, to my mind, exactly right.
Dickens gives him his dignity back, at the last.
And the suit, of course, consumes itself in the same moment. The costs devour the entire estate.
There was nothing to inherit. There never was. The lawyers' fees have consumed everything Jarndyce and Jarndyce ever promised.
The cruelty of that timing — that Richard dies learning the case is resolved, but resolved into nothing — is almost too precise to be borne.
It is Dickens at his most satirical and his most compassionate simultaneously.
That convergence — the suit resolving into nothing at the very moment Richard is dying — is one of the great structural ironies of nineteenth-century fiction.
And I think what this conversation has shown is that the novel refuses to let us settle the question of blame.
Edmund sees a moral weakness that Chancery exploits. James sees an institution so pathological it would corrupt anyone. Caroline sees a man who — at the end — knows himself at last.
And perhaps the greatness of Bleak House is that it insists on all three at once.
We'll be back after a short break to look at what I think is the novel's other great unraveling — the mystery of Lady Dedlock — and what its resolution costs everyone who loves her.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take Dickens' great sprawling masterpiece apart, chapter by chapter, theme by theme.
Today we turn to one of the novel's most haunting figures — a woman who is simultaneously everywhere and nowhere in her own story.
Lady Dedlock: aristocrat, ice-queen, secret-keeper, and, as we'll discover, one of the most psychologically complex characters Dickens ever created.
I'm joined today by three people who've thought deeply about this novel and who will, I suspect, disagree with each other in the most illuminating ways.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong engagement with Dickens is grounded in moral philosophy and a deep suspicion of politicised readings.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows more about the Court of Chancery than most Victorian barristers did — and what it meant to be trapped by it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House five times and still stops cold at certain sentences — which is exactly the kind of reader this novel deserves.
Lady Dedlock's identity is a kind of phantom — constructed, performed, and finally shattered.
Edmund, shall we start with you — where does the performance begin?
The performance begins, I would argue, before the novel does.
Lady Dedlock arrives in our imaginations already fully formed — already glacial, already magnificent, already bored.
Dickens introduces her at Chesney Wold with that extraordinary description — the world around her seems to reflect her inner condition.
He writes that she is 'perfectly well-bred' and that 'she has a manner of her own' — which is Dickens' way of saying she is entirely impenetrable.
That impermeability is the first thing to understand — she has constructed a self that no one is permitted to touch.
Burke wrote of the aristocratic manner as a kind of social contract — you maintain the form, the form maintains the order.
Lady Dedlock has taken that contract and made it her prison.
Prison is exactly the word, and I don't think it's accidental that Dickens opens the novel with two kinds of fog — the fog outside and the fog inside Lady Dedlock.
What strikes me every time I re-read those early chapters is the boredom — the famous, terrible boredom.
Dickens writes of her being 'at the centre of the fashionable intelligence' and yet she finds everything 'wearisome' — which is not laziness, it's grief with nowhere to go.
She has suppressed something so enormous that the suppression has become her entire personality.
And then comes that magnificent, terrifying moment in chapter two — when she sees Nemo's handwriting on the legal documents.
Everything she has built over twenty years cracks open in a single instant.
Tulkinghorn notices, and the reader notices, and Lady Dedlock herself notices that she has been noticed — and that is the beginning of the end.
I want to press on what that moment actually means — legally, socially, existentially.
The handwriting on the affidavit belongs to Nemo — which is Latin for 'no one,' and that is not a coincidence.
Captain Hawdon has erased himself from legal and social existence just as Lady Dedlock has erased her past self.
They are mirror phantoms — two people who have performed non-existence in order to survive.
And what Dickens understood, with extraordinary clarity, is that Victorian legal identity was deeply material — your name on a document was your existence.
Nemo's handwriting resurfaces in a Chancery document — the very institution that grinds down identity and reduces persons to case numbers.
Lady Dedlock's suppressed identity doesn't resurface through emotion first — it resurfaces through a legal document. That is Dickens at his most precise.
Blackstone makes an important point, though I'd frame it differently.
What Dickens is showing us is not primarily a critique of legal institutions — it is a study in the consequences of a lie sustained too long.
Lady Dedlock made a choice — or rather, she submitted to a world that gave her no good choices — and she has been paying the compound interest on that choice ever since.
Dr. Johnson observed that the chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken — and that is Lady Dedlock's predicament precisely.
The performance of Lady Dedlock has become so total that even she can no longer locate the woman underneath it.

When she says to Esther, 'I am your wicked and unhappy mother,' it is one of the most devastating sentences in the English novel — because it is the first true sentence she has spoken in twenty years.
Twenty years of perfect performance, and then — that.
That scene in the garden — the recognition scene between Esther and Lady Dedlock — I find it almost unbearable to read.
Because Dickens gives Lady Dedlock a moment of absolute nakedness, and then immediately begins the process of putting the mask back on.
She tells Esther — and I'm paraphrasing here — that they must never meet again as mother and daughter, that the world must never know.
And what's extraordinary is that Esther agrees — out of love, out of a kind of terrible selflessness that is both beautiful and heartbreaking.
Two women choosing silence to protect each other — and the silence will destroy them both.
Dickens understood something very specific about how women were compelled to perform their own erasure — and Lady Dedlock is the most extreme embodiment of that.
I think we need to say something about Tulkinghorn, because he is the mechanism by which Lady Dedlock's phantom identity is dismantled.
He is a lawyer of the old school — keeper of secrets, servant of families, but ultimately servant of power.
What makes him so chilling is that he has no discernible motive beyond accumulation — he collects secrets the way other men collect property.
Dickens describes his chambers at the Temple as being entirely without comfort — 'iron-bound' is the phrase that sticks in my mind — as if he himself is a legal document rather than a man.
And the historical reality is that lawyers like Tulkinghorn genuinely held families at their mercy — the solicitor was often the only person who knew where every skeleton was buried.
Lady Dedlock's downfall is not simply personal tragedy — it is a systemic consequence of how Victorian society stored and weaponised private information.
I'll grant Blackstone the systemic point — but I'd resist turning Tulkinghorn into a mere symptom.
He is a magnificently drawn character in his own right — a study in will entirely divorced from conscience.
And Lady Dedlock's final flight — her disguising herself as a servant, her wandering through the slums, her death at the gate of the pauper's graveyard — that is not systemic consequence.
That is a woman dismantling every layer of the identity she has constructed, one by one, until she reaches the absolute zero of her original shame.
She dies as she lived before Sir Leicester — as a woman outside the walls, unknown and unclaimed.
The death at the graveyard gate — I have to say something about that, because the prose there is extraordinary.
When Esther and Bucket finally find her, Dickens writes — and I want to get this exactly right — that Esther sees someone 'lying on the steps' who she first takes for Jenny, the brickmaker's wife.
'I looked at her. She lay there, who had so long been pursued. Cold and dead.'
Those three final words — cold and dead — land like a verdict, like a sentence handed down by the novel itself.
And the fact that Esther almost mistakes her for a working-class woman — because Lady Dedlock has dressed as one in her flight — is Dickens being precise about identity and disguise.
In death, the performance finally dissolves — and what's left is just a woman.
And she dies in the shadow of the graveyard where Nemo — Hawdon — is buried.
That is not accidental geography — Dickens is closing a circle.
The two erased people, the two performed non-existences, are reunited in the most squalid corner of London — the very inversion of the social world they both inhabited and were destroyed by.
And Jo the crossing-sweeper — who has been moving through this story like a ghost himself — Jo had tended to Nemo's grave.
The least visible person in the novel turns out to be the keeper of the most important secret geography.
That image — the erased reunited in erasure — feels like a good place to pause and take stock of what we've been circling.
Lady Dedlock is, in some ways, the novel's central tragedy — and yet Dickens keeps her at a remove for much of the book.
Edmund, is that distance a flaw, or is it the whole point?
It is entirely the point — and it is one of Dickens' most daring structural choices.
We receive Lady Dedlock almost entirely through the eyes of others — through Esther's wonder, through Tulkinghorn's cold surveillance, through Sir Leicester's adoration.
She never narrates — and that silence is itself the most eloquent thing about her.
The novel has two narrative streams — Esther's first-person account and the third-person omniscient narrator.
And Lady Dedlock falls between them — she belongs to neither, and that formal exclusion mirrors her psychological condition exactly.
That's beautifully put, and it's why the letter she leaves for Sir Leicester is so shattering.
It's the one moment she speaks in her own prose — and it's a farewell.
She gives Sir Leicester the only thing she can — the truth — but she delivers it in the form of an exit.
And Sir Leicester's response — his immediate, unconditional forgiveness — is one of the things that makes Bleak House more complicated than a simple satire.
Dickens gives the aristocrat a great soul — and gives him the devastating irony that the soul arrives too late to save anyone.
Sir Leicester is a fascinating case precisely because Dickens refuses to make him simply ridiculous.
He is pompous, he is unreflective about privilege, he genuinely believes the established order is the natural order.
And yet when the test comes — real, personal, shattering — he passes it with more honour than most of the professional men around him.
The stroke he suffers when he learns of Lady Dedlock's flight is rendered by Dickens as a kind of heroism — the man who can no longer speak makes it understood that she is to be found and forgiven.
It is one of the novel's most quietly radical arguments — that love, even aristocratic love, can transcend the social machinery that produced it.
I think we could spend another hour just on Sir Leicester — and perhaps we will, in a later episode.
But what strikes me listening to all three of you is how thoroughly Lady Dedlock's phantom identity implicates everyone around her — Esther, Tulkinghorn, Sir Leicester, even Hawdon in his grave.
She is a secret that the whole novel organises itself around — and when the secret is finally out, the novel loses something along with her.
Caroline — last word on Lady Dedlock, for now.
What do we take away?
We take away — I think — a portrait of what happens when a person is required to perform a self that has nothing to do with who they actually are.
And Dickens is precise about where that requirement comes from — it comes from a society that cannot accommodate a fallen woman, a woman with a past, a woman who loved outside the rules.
The boredom, the coldness, the magnificence — all of it is the armour of someone who stopped being allowed to feel.
And in the end she can only reclaim herself by shedding everything — the title, the house, the clothes, the name.
She dies in a stranger's clothes, at a pauper's gate, and she has never been more entirely herself.
She has never been more entirely herself — that is a remarkable place to land, and exactly the kind of paradox this novel lives for.
Coming up, we turn to the other great mystery at the heart of Bleak House — the Court of Chancery itself, and what it does to the people who fall into it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: A Boy in the Streets: Jo's Testimony

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel seriously — one chapter, one character, one injustice at a time.
I'm your host, and today we're spending time with what I think is the most morally urgent figure in the entire book — a crossing-sweeper named Jo.
Jo doesn't know his age, his parents, or his letters.
He sweeps a crossing in the shadow of the law courts, and Dickens uses him to put a single question to Victorian England — and arguably to us.
Joining me today are three people who have thought long and hard about this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a novel of character and moral imagination — and who keeps a healthy scepticism about readings that reduce Dickens to a pamphleteer.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows what Chancery and the Poor Law actually were — and what they did to real people who looked very much like Jo.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel five times and still cries at the same passages.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin at the beginning of Jo's story — or rather, at the inquest in chapter eleven, where Dickens first forces us to pay attention to him.
Jo's first appearance at the inquest into Nemo's death is one of Dickens' most brilliantly calculated scenes.
A coroner's inquest was a formal legal proceeding with quite specific rules about witness competence — and one of those rules was that witnesses had to understand the nature of an oath.
Jo, when asked whether he knows what an oath is, simply doesn't.
He is therefore ruled incompetent as a witness and dismissed — which Dickens presents, with devastating understatement, as a perfectly ordinary outcome.
And it was ordinary.
Children in Jo's position were routinely excluded from legal testimony on exactly these grounds.
The system had no mechanism for accounting for the fact that its own failures had produced his ignorance.
And Dickens catches that circularity with horrible precision.
What strikes me most about the inquest scene, and indeed about Jo throughout, is Dickens' absolute formal control.
There is a temptation to read Jo purely as a piece of social argument — and he is that, I grant Blackstone his point.
But Dickens is also doing something more primary.
He is giving Jo a voice — a specific, irreducible, dignified voice — precisely so that the reader cannot dismiss him as an abstraction.
Think of that extraordinary passage in chapter sixteen, where Dickens addresses the reader directly — the famous apostrophe to Jo.
"Jo, my poor Jo, it is a terrible day when the law of this great land so deals with a creature like yourself."
Now, that is not the narrator addressing a social type.
That is a human being addressing another human being, across the full distance of class and literacy and fortune.
Edmund, yes — and the thing that breaks me every time is that Dickens earns that apostrophe.
He doesn't simply ask us to feel for Jo.
He makes us listen to him first.
That inquest testimony — the way Jo tries to describe what he knows about Nemo — is written in a dialect so precise and so innocent that it becomes a kind of poetry.
Dickens gives us Jo saying something like — and I'll read this as carefully as I can — he says about Nemo:
"He wos wery good to me, he wos."
That's all Jo has to offer as testimony.
And it is, by any humane measure, the most important thing said at that inquest.
Caroline puts her finger on something historically precise, actually.
What Jo knows about Nemo is that he was kind to him.
He doesn't know where he came from, he doesn't know his real name, he doesn't know anything the law considers relevant.
But in the world Jo inhabits — Tom-all-Alone's, the streets around Lincoln's Inn — what matters is whether someone treated you decently.
That's a different epistemology entirely.
And Dickens — who understood the street from his own childhood — recognised that Jo's knowledge, his form of knowing, was not inferior.
It was simply invisible to the institutions that claimed to govern his life.
Invisible is the word, isn't it.
And that invisibility has a geography — it's centred on Tom-all-Alone's, the ruined slum that Dickens returns to again and again.
Edmund, what do you make of Tom-all-Alone's as a literary construction?
Tom-all-Alone's is one of the most extraordinary pieces of naming in English fiction.
The name itself tells you everything — it is a place defined by abandonment, by the absence of community, by a solitude imposed rather than chosen.
And Dickens makes explicit — in one of those passages of great controlled anger — that Tom-all-Alone's is directly produced by the Court of Chancery.
The land is tied up in litigation, therefore it cannot be improved, therefore it rots, therefore Jo lives there — moving on, always moving on.
There is a passage — chapter forty-six, I believe — where Dickens addresses the slum directly, and it is one of those moments where his prose rises to something close to prophetic fury.
"Tom has his revenge.
Even the winds are his messengers, and they serve him in these hours of darkness.
When from every corner comes a breath of pestilence, through the foul and fetid air he disperses."
That's disease as political argument.
The smallpox Jo carries is not merely tragic — it is the slum's answer to the society that created it.
And that pestilence lands on Esther.
Which is — I mean, structurally, that is Dickens at his most ruthless.
Esther is the character we trust most, the most morally luminous person in the book.
And Jo — who has been moved on by every authority, who belongs nowhere — Jo infects her.
The disease crosses the full width of the social world.
And before that happens, there's the moment where Jo and Esther and Allan Woodcourt encounter each other in the street, and Jo is almost delirious, being moved on as usual.
And Jo says — this is chapter forty-seven — something that has always undone me completely.
"I'm moving on.
I'm always a-moving on, sar."
That repetition.
That small word — always.
"Move on" is almost certainly the phrase Dickens knew from his journalism and from police court reporting.
It was the standard instruction given by police constables to anyone loitering — which in practice meant anyone poor, anyone homeless, anyone without a fixed address.
You could not stand still.
There was no place in the legal or social geography of London where a Jo was permitted to simply exist.
And what Dickens does — with devastating economy — is take that administrative phrase and show us what it means to have internalised it.
Jo doesn't resist, doesn't resent.
He has absorbed the instruction as a description of his own nature.
That is extraordinary — that the most violent thing the system does to Jo is make him unable to imagine an alternative to movement.
And then, of course, he stops moving.
Edmund, can we talk about Jo's death — the deathbed scene in chapter forty-seven?
Jo's death is, I would argue without apology, one of the great passages in the English novel.
Allan Woodcourt sits with Jo at the end and tries — tries — to teach him the Lord's Prayer.
Jo has never heard it.
He repeats each phrase after Woodcourt — haltingly, not fully understanding — and it is one of the most quietly devastating acts of human connection in all of Dickens.
And then Dickens steps in, with that authorial voice, and delivers what amounts to a controlled explosion.
"Dead, your Majesty.
Dead, my lords and gentlemen.
Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order.
Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts.
And dying thus around us every day."
The anaphora — Dead, dead, dead — is a funeral toll, yes.
But it is also a roll call of the guilty.
I cannot read that passage without my voice breaking.
And I think what makes it almost unbearable is the specificity of the address.
Dickens doesn't say "society" or "the age" — he says Your Majesty, my lords and gentlemen, Right Reverends.
He names the people who had the power to prevent this death.
And then — and this is what I think people sometimes miss — he includes us.
"Men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts."
That's the reader.
Dickens is indicting us too — for reading and feeling and doing nothing.
The historical context for that death makes it more, not less, devastating.
By the time Bleak House was published in serial form between 1852 and 1853, the arguments for sanitary reform had been made, loudly, for nearly a decade.
Edwin Chadwick's report on the sanitary conditions of the labouring population had come out in 1842.
The connection between filth, poverty, and disease was known.
What was lacking was not knowledge but will — political will, specifically among those Dickens addresses: lords, legislators, clergy.
And Jo is dying of a disease — smallpox — that was already, in principle, preventable.
That is the depth of the accusation.
I want to resist the reading of Jo as purely an accusatory device, however.
Blackstone is right about the political charge, and I don't wish to diminish it.
But what saves Jo from being a mere exhibit in an argument is his particularity.
He has opinions.
He is capable of loyalty — his devotion to Nemo's memory is unwavering and deeply felt.
He is confused and frightened by the mysterious woman who asks him to show her where Nemo lived and is buried — Lady Dedlock, though he cannot know that.
He is, in short, a person.
And Dickens insists on that personhood with every verbal detail — the dialect, the bewilderment, the small acts of gratitude.
That scene with the veiled lady — Lady Dedlock disguised — is one of the great uncanny scenes in the novel.
Because Jo doesn't know who she is.
But the reader does — or begins to suspect.
And there is something about watching Jo try to make sense of this grand, grief-stricken woman kneeling at a pauper's grave that is — I don't have a better word than heartbreaking.
Jo registers that she is not like the other people who come to him.
She pays him — unusually generously — and he is grateful, and confused, and oddly tender about it.
And what Dickens understands — this is where his genius resides, for me — is that even the most dispossessed child has the capacity to perceive human grief.
That perception — Jo as a kind of unlikely witness to the whole novel's hidden story — brings us, I think, to a final question.
Dickens says somewhere that Jo is one of the many thousands who are dying around us every day — a recurring phrase, a deliberate haunting.
What do we take from Jo today?
James — you've thought most directly about this.
What I take from Jo is the reminder that systemic failure is not abstract.
It lands on specific people with specific names — or in Jo's case, without a last name, without a birth record, without a school place.
And the terrifying thing about Dickens' argument — delivered through Jo's very existence — is that the system doesn't hate Jo.
It simply has no category for him.
And that — the indifference, not the malice — is what Dickens found most monstrous.
I would add only this.
Burke wrote that society is a contract between the dead, the living, and those yet to be born.
Jo is evidence of what happens when one party to that contract is simply omitted — when the living forget their obligation to those who come after.
Dickens and Burke, on that point, are not as far apart as one might think.
For me, Jo endures because he is the novel's conscience made flesh.
Every time the plot threatens to become about inheritance or secrets or the romance of Esther and Woodcourt — and those things matter — Jo pulls us back.
Back to the crossing.
Back to the boy who is always moving on.
Always moving on.

We'll pause there — on that image — and when we return, we'll turn to the other great institution at the heart of this novel: the Court of Chancery, and what Jarndyce and Jarndyce means for everyone caught in its orbit.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Wit and Folly in the Law

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, with Esther, with the labyrinthine corridors of Chancery as a system.
Now I want to turn to something that Dickens does that I think is sometimes underestimated — the sheer comedy of it all.
Because Bleak House is, among many other things, an extraordinarily funny book.
And the wit is sharpest, I think, when it is aimed directly at the law.
Edmund, you've written about Dickens's satirical method — where does the comedy in Bleak House sit for you?
One must begin by insisting on a distinction that lazy readers often miss.
Dickens is not merely a satirist of institutions.
He is a satirist of human vanity — and the institutions are simply where that vanity finds its most elaborate costuming.
Consider Mr. Tulkinghorn.
He is not comic in the least — he is genuinely sinister.
But then consider the aptly named Mr. Vholes, Richard Carstone's attorney, with his — and this is Dickens at his most precisely horrible — his two daughters and an aged father in the Vale of Taunton.
Dickens writes of Vholes that he is 'a sallow man with pinched lips' who gives 'legal opinion as if he were tasting bad cheese.'
The comedy is inseparable from the menace, which is rather the point.
Vholes is funny precisely because he is consuming Richard Carstone from the inside out, with perfect legal propriety.
That image of Vholes is one I come back to every single time I re-read the book.
There's a passage where Dickens describes him removing his close black gloves slowly, as if he were skinning his hands.
And then he says something like — let me get this right —
'The name of Vholes, at once professional and ominous, has a relish of the tomb about it.'
A relish of the tomb! That's so wickedly good.
Dickens gives you that Gothic shudder and then winks at you at the same time.
And what's devastating is that every letter Vholes writes costs Richard money — money he doesn't have.
The Vholes portrait is actually one of Dickens's most historically precise caricatures.
The solicitor who attaches himself to a Chancery suitor and bills for every breath was not a Dickensian invention — it was a documented grievance before parliamentary committees throughout the 1840s.
But what Dickens adds — and this is where the wit becomes something more than wit — is the defence that the novel puts in Vholes's own mouth.
Dickens has Vholes justify himself by saying he has 'a father to support, and two daughters.'
And then Dickens — with breathtaking irony — notes that society finds this perfectly sufficient justification for the whole system.
The joke is on all of us, not merely on Vholes.
Blackstone puts his finger on something important there.
The genius of Dickens is that his most savage satire is delivered in the blandest possible prose register.
One thinks particularly of the great set-piece of the opening chapter — the description of the Lord Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery.
Dickens writes of Jarndyce and Jarndyce as a case that has 'in the course of time become so complicated, that no man alive knows what it means.'
Now that is not merely a satirical observation — it is a philosophically devastating one.
A system so complex that its own practitioners have lost the thread — Burke would have called it an inheritance nobody can read.
I want to bring in a figure we haven't mentioned yet — Mr. Skimpole.
Because he seems to me a different kind of folly in the book — not a legal folly but a moral one dressed in wit.
Caroline, you've always had strong feelings about Skimpole.
Strong feelings is putting it mildly.
Harold Skimpole is one of Dickens's most brilliant and most troubling comic creations.
He presents himself as a child — his whole personality is constructed around a refusal of adult responsibility.
And he does it with such wit, such genuine charm, that Esther almost forgives him even as he betrays Jo to Bucket.
There's a line where Skimpole explains that money is something he has absolutely no business with —
'It is a thing,' he says, 'of no moment to me. I don't understand it. I never could.'
And the horror is that Dickens makes this charming — genuinely, seductively charming — right up until the moment you realize it is also monstrous.
Skimpole is interesting to me precisely because he performs the role of the artistic innocent — a kind of legal fiction of personhood.
He claims the immunity of a child while exercising the cunning of a thoroughly adult operator.
In a sense, Skimpole is a human version of what Chancery does structurally — it diffuses responsibility so completely that no individual can be blamed.
When Jo dies — and he dies in large part because Skimpole turned him over for a five-pound note — who exactly is responsible?
The law would say nobody. And that, I think, is Dickens's deepest joke — and his deepest fury.
I find myself in partial agreement with Blackstone, which is unusual enough to be worth recording.
Skimpole is a study in what one might call willed irresponsibility — a form of moral cowardice dressed as aesthetic sensibility.
But I would resist the structural reading.
Dickens is not diagnosing a system — he is diagnosing a soul.
And the comedy of Skimpole is that he has — with great ingenuity and considerable effort — dismantled his own soul piece by piece, and calls it freedom.
That's beautifully put — and it makes me think of Krook, who is in some ways the comic obverse of Skimpole.
Where Skimpole performs ignorance as freedom, Krook hoards knowledge as power.
He calls his shop the Court of Chancery — he says it himself, quite cheerfully.
He says — and this is one of my favourite moments of dark comedy in the whole book —
'I have so many things here, of so many kinds, and I can't tell what I've got or what I haven't.'
Which is a perfect description of the Court of Chancery itself — an institution that has accumulated so much that it can no longer see what it holds.
And of course Krook's end — spontaneous combustion — is itself a kind of savage juridical joke.
The system doesn't reform — it simply explodes from within.
James — a last thought on where Dickens's legal wit ultimately lands?
It lands, I think, in the most uncomfortable place possible — not with the villains but with the bystanders.
Dickens opens the novel with a narrator who is almost lyrically amused by the fog, by the mud, by the absurdity of it all.
But by the time Jo dies, the tone has shifted entirely — and Dickens points the finger directly at the reader.
He writes, in that extraordinary apostrophe, 'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order.'
The wit has become an indictment — and the folly being exposed is not merely Chancery's, but ours.
Dead. And yet the novel lives on — precisely because Dickens's laughter never lets us look away.

We'll be back after the break to look more closely at how the novel's two narrators — Esther's intimate voice and the third-person narrator's gothic sweep — hold this whole brilliant, maddening world together.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the greatest English novels and gives it the time it deserves.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be reading Dickens' vast, magnificent, infuriating masterpiece together.
Bleak House is a novel about fog — moral, legal, atmospheric — and about what happens to ordinary people when institutions designed to serve them instead consume them.
To help us unpick it, I'm joined by three readers whose knowledge and passion for this novel I trust absolutely.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens scholars of his generation.
Edmund reads Bleak House as a novel about character — about the moral choices individuals make in the face of systems designed to grind them down.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career studying Victorian institutions — Chancery among them.
James brings the documentary record: what these courts and workhouses actually were, and what they actually did to real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
Caroline cares above all about the experience of reading — the sentence that makes you stop, the passage you read aloud to whoever happens to be nearby.
Today we're beginning with the architecture of corruption — the way Dickens constructs, brick by deliberate brick, a world in which the rot is not incidental but structural.
Edmund, the novel opens with one of the most famous paragraphs in Victorian fiction — that description of fog over London and the Court of Chancery sitting at its heart.
What do you make of Dickens' choice to begin there?
It is, I think, one of the most audacious openings in the English novel — and I use that word with care.
Dickens does not begin with a character, or a family, or even a story.
He begins with a condition — the condition of England, if you will — rendered as meteorological event.
The fog is not merely atmosphere.
It is a statement about epistemology — about what can be known, and by whom, and at what cost.
Dickens writes — and one ought to hear these words carefully — that the fog is 'everywhere.'
'Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
That word 'defiled' is doing extraordinary work.
The fog is not merely dirty — it is morally contaminated, and the contamination flows from the city outward.
Now, I know my colleagues may wish to press that into the service of a political argument.
But I would suggest the fog is first and foremost a literary achievement — a device of extraordinary structural intelligence.
I take Edmund's point about the literary achievement — it is a magnificent set-piece.
But I think we have to be honest about the fact that Dickens had a specific target in his sights, and that target was the Court of Chancery.
The real Court of Chancery, by the 1850s, had cases that had been running for forty, fifty, sixty years.
There are documented instances of suitors — real people, not fictional ones — who died waiting for a verdict.
Dickens knew this, and he places the fog directly over the court — not over Parliament, not over the Bank of England, but over Chancery.
He then writes that the Lord High Chancellor sits 'in the midst of the mud and at the heart of the fog.'
'On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be sitting here — as here he is.'
That 'as here he is' — three plain words — is a prosecutorial jab.
Dickens is saying: this is not satire, not exaggeration — this is documentary.
And the history bears him out entirely.
What strikes me, coming at this from the reader's angle, is how the opening prepares you for a kind of dizziness.
You can't get your footing in that first chapter.
And I think that's entirely deliberate — Dickens is staging your disorientation as a reader to mirror the experience of anyone caught in the court.
There's that wonderful passage where Dickens piles on the mud — mud everywhere, as if the land had just emerged from a flood.

'As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.'
A Megalosaurus on Holborn Hill!
It is absurd, it is funny, and it is deeply serious all at once.
The world of Chancery is prehistoric — it has not evolved, it waddles, it is grotesquely out of place in a modern city.
That image sets the satirical temperature for everything that follows.
Caroline's point about the satirical temperature is well made — though I'd press her on the word 'absurd.'
The Megalosaurus is grotesque, yes, but Dickens is not writing in the mode of Swiftian contempt.
There is something almost elegiac about it — as though Dickens genuinely mourns what institutions were supposed to be, before they became what they are.
Consider Jarndyce and Jarndyce itself — that great spectral suit.
Dickens tells us it is 'a cause that could not be defined, a will that could not be proved, estates that could not be established.'
The triple negation is the point.
Chancery is a system constituted by its own incapacity to conclude.
And it is that incapacity — not any villain's malice — which is the true corruption Dickens anatomises.
Edmund's phrase — 'constituted by its own incapacity to conclude' — is an excellent description of what Chancery actually was.
The fees were generated by delay.
Every motion, every filing, every reference to a Master — each produced its charge, its counter-charge, its solicitor's bill.
The reformers of the 1850s — and Dickens was effectively one of them, through journalism as much as fiction — calculated that Chancery costs routinely consumed the very estate being litigated.
Which is precisely what happens to Jarndyce and Jarndyce in the novel.
The suit ends not with a verdict but with the lawyers' announcement that the costs have absorbed the whole of the estate.
The system did not fail — it performed exactly as designed.
And what I find so painful — on every re-reading — is what that system does to the people caught inside it.
Richard Carstone is the heartbreak at the centre of that argument.
He is a young man of genuine warmth and ability — Esther loves him, Ada loves him — and the suit hollows him out from the inside.
Jarndyce says of him, with such quiet sorrow, that the suit has 'engendered or confirmed in him a habit of putting off.'
'In the meantime, the great suit sleeps sometimes for years, sometimes for months; awakens and disappears again; and so wears out hundreds of people.'
'Wears out' — that's exactly it.
Chancery doesn't destroy people in one blow — it exhausts them, incrementally, until there's nothing left.
And Richard's tragedy is that he can't stop hoping.
That is the precise point at which I would gently resist a purely systemic reading.
Richard is not merely a victim of Chancery.
He is a young man who chooses, repeatedly and against all counsel, to invest his identity in a fantasy of inheritance.
Jarndyce — who is himself a product of the same suit — does not succumb.
The distinction is moral, not sociological.
Jarndyce tells Esther — I think in one of the great plain sentences of the novel — 'Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts.'
'Never trust in Chancery.'
That is the counsel of a man who has understood the system and refused to be defined by it.
Richard cannot receive that counsel.
And that incapacity is Richard's tragedy — not Chancery's crime.
I have a great deal of respect for that reading, Edmund, but I think it lets the institution off rather too lightly.
Jarndyce is a rare figure — a man of independent means and exceptional self-knowledge.
Most people caught in Chancery were not Jarndyces.
Think of Miss Flite — that heartbreaking little figure who has attended the court every day for years, waiting for a judgement she calls 'Ashes, Ruin, Dust, Despair.'
She keeps birds in cages — and names them after the outcomes of Chancery.
'Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death, Cunning, Folly, Words, Wigs, Rags, Sheepskin, Plunder, Precedent, Jargon, Gammon, and Spinach.'
That list begins with hope and ends with spinach — which is either bathetic comedy or the most despairing thing in Victorian fiction.
Miss Flite is not a woman of weak will.
She is a woman the system has driven mad.
And then there is Krook.
If we're talking about the architecture of corruption, Krook is the building itself.
He runs his rag-and-bottle shop with all the chaotic obscurity of Chancery — he even calls himself the Lord Chancellor.
He has papers everywhere, documents he cannot read — because he is illiterate — but will not let anyone else read either.
Dickens describes his shop as 'a little, mad, comical, horrible place.'
Those four adjectives together — little, mad, comical, horrible — that's the whole tonal register of the novel in miniature.
And Krook's end — spontaneous combustion — is the most outrageous, the most defended, and in some ways the most perfect thing in the book.
Corruption literally consumes itself from within.
Spontaneous combustion is the one point on which I find Dickens least defensible as a realist — and most magnificent as a symbolist.
Lewes attacked him for it in the press, and Dickens responded with characteristic tenacity in his Preface — citing actual documented cases.
Whether one finds those cases convincing is beside the point.
The point is what the image achieves: a system so saturated in corruption that it cannot sustain itself.
Burke would have understood it perfectly.
We've moved from fog to fire — which feels like exactly the right trajectory for a novel this relentless.
What I'm hearing is a kind of argument about whether corruption in Bleak House is systemic or moral — whether it lives in institutions or in people.
And I suspect Dickens' answer is: both, and each makes the other worse.
In our next segment, we'll descend from the fog of Chancery into something even darker — the world of Tom-all-Alone's, and the figure of Jo the crossing-sweeper.
Because if Chancery is the architecture of corruption, Jo is the human cost — the smallest, most overlooked brick in the wall.
We've spent this episode deep inside the machinery of Bleak House — the fog, the law, the characters who survive and those who don't.
I want to close by stepping back and asking the bigger question: how does Dickens actually build this world?
Not what it means — but how it is made.
Caroline, you've lived with this novel longer than any of us around this table.
Where would you start?
I'd start with the very first word.
The novel opens with 'London,' stated flat, with no verb, no qualification.
And then immediately — fog.
Dickens gives you a word for the place, and then he immediately obscures it.
That is the whole novel in miniature, really.
He names things with absolute precision and then shows you how little the name tells you.
The fog pours into Lincoln's Inn Hall, it creeps along the river, it settles on the Essex marshes.
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
That anaphora — 'fog, fog, fog' — it isn't decoration.
It's the rhythm of an institution that has been repeating itself for generations.
Caroline is right about the precision, but I think the fog serves a moral as much as an atmospheric function.
Dickens was not, at root, a polemicist.
He was a moralist — in the great tradition of Fielding, of Johnson.
The world of Bleak House is built, above all, through character.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is the mechanism, but it is Esther who is the centre of gravity.
She builds her world sentence by sentence — through that quietly extraordinary voice of hers.
'I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever.'
That self-deprecation, of course, is the subtlest form of authority Dickens ever invented.
We trust Esther precisely because she does not trust herself.
I take Edmund's point about character, but I'd argue the world-building here is fundamentally institutional.
Dickens understood something that very few novelists have ever grasped: that institutions have their own personality.
Chancery is not a backdrop.
It is a character — one that feeds, that delays, that destroys, with perfect bureaucratic indifference.
And what Dickens understood about that indifference is extraordinary.
'The one great principle of the English law is, to make business for itself.'
That is not satire for its own sake.
It is a sociological observation of the first order, and it holds as well today as it did in 1852.
The world of Bleak House is built from the collision of vulnerable individuals with that impersonal machinery.
What I keep coming back to is the double narrative — the two voices, the two styles.
Esther's first-person warmth alongside the third-person narrator's cold, scalding irony.
Together they create a kind of stereoscopic vision of the world.
The third-person narrator is withering about Mrs. Jellyby, about Skimpole, about the whole scaffolding of Victorian self-congratulation.
But Esther — Esther finds something to love, or at least to pity, in nearly everyone she meets.
That tension — between condemnation and compassion — is where the world of the novel lives.
The double narrative is, I think, the greatest formal achievement of Victorian fiction.
And one still insufficiently appreciated.
What strikes me, finally, about how Dickens builds this world is the sheer density of connection.
Everyone is linked — Esther to Lady Dedlock, Jo to Nemo, Tulkinghorn to Bucket, Bucket to everyone.
The novel argues, structurally, that we are all implicated in one another's fates.
That is not a political argument.
It is a deeply, profoundly moral one.
I won't quarrel with Edmund on the moral dimension — but I'd say the two are inseparable here.
The world-building of Bleak House is so powerful because the structure of the novel mirrors the structure of society.
People at the top — the Dedlocks, the Lord Chancellor — believe themselves to be untouched by the fog.
But the fog reaches everywhere.
Jo sweeps his crossing, Lady Dedlock dies in the snow outside a burial ground — they are connected.
The novel's world is built on that terrible, irrefutable connective tissue.
Fog, character, institution, connection — and running beneath all of it, that extraordinary double voice.
I think what this conversation has revealed is that you cannot isolate any one of those elements.
Bleak House works because they are all working at once — simultaneously, in concert.
Edmund, James, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure thinking through this novel with you.
Bleak House was published in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853, and it has never stopped being current.
That, perhaps, is the final measure of how well Dickens built his world.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.
